summary.text: A 37-year-old woman with short stature (height 3.5 feet) presented to the outpatient department with gradual, progressive, painless loss of vision in the right eye for the past three months. She denied systemic illnesses, previous ocular complaints and medication use, and no other family member had similar features. Visual acuity was 1/60 right and 6/18 left.

Examination showed intraocular pressure of 17 mmHg in both eyes, early bilateral posterior subcapsular cataracts, subretinal fluid at the macula and a shallow exudative retinal detachment in the right eye, with a normal left fundus; a provisional diagnosis of exudative retinal detachment secondary to central serous chorioretinopathy was made. OCT, angiography and B-scan ultrasonography supported the findings, and cortisol, growth hormone, prolactin and electrolytes were normal.

She was referred to an endocrinologist and declined a brain MRI. Oral mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist therapy at 50 mg daily was started, named eplerenone in the case text and spironolactone in the abstract, without laser or photodynamic therapy. Subretinal fluid fell and acuity reached 6/24 within two months, then 6/18 with complete resolution of the exudative detachment after three months.

At six months right eye visual acuity was 6/12 with complete anatomical recovery and stable retinal findings, and she remains under periodic review including monitoring of cataract progression. The authors describe a good response to eplerenone monotherapy.
